title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 40
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Going Up
passages.text:
A. Tall buildings were not made possible by the ability to lift materials or to build high, both of which existed long before them. What limited height was the willingness of people to climb: above about six storeys, upper floors were cheap, undesirable and used for storage or for the poorest tenants, and no amount of structural capability changed that. The constraint was human legs, and it was removed by machinery rather than by engineering of the building itself.

B. The device that removed it was not the hoist but the safety catch. Hoists for goods had existed for a long time and nobody would ride one, because a broken rope meant a fall; a mechanism that grips the guide rails automatically if the rope fails converted an unacceptable risk into an acceptable one. The invention that mattered was a brake, and its public demonstration was as important as the mechanism, since the problem being solved was partly one of belief.

C. The consequence for buildings was an inversion of value that persists. Once vertical movement was effortless, the upper floors gained light, quiet and a view, and became the most valuable rather than the least; the top of the building, formerly the servants' quarters and the store rooms, became the expensive part. Rent gradients within buildings turned upside down within a generation.

D. Height then ran into a different limit, which is the lifts themselves. A tall building needs many lifts, each occupying a shaft on every floor it serves, and the shafts consume floor area that cannot be let — so beyond a certain height, each additional storey requires more shaft than it provides usable space. Skyscrapers are shaped by this arithmetic, which is why they taper and why express lifts serve zones rather than every floor.

E. Steel and glass changed how the building carried itself rather than how tall it could be. Hanging a light skin on a frame that carries the load allowed thin exterior walls, more window area and much faster construction, and it made the tall building economically repeatable rather than exceptional. The visual language everyone now associates with height is a consequence of load being moved from the wall to the frame.

F. What determines whether such buildings make sense is not engineering at all. They are expensive per unit of floor area, they concentrate people in ways that require substantial transport capacity, and they are built where land prices justify the cost — which means their appearance in a city is a statement about land values rather than about ambition. Where they are built without those land values, they are usually monuments rather than accommodation.

passages.title: Deciding Whether It Works
passages.text:
The randomised trial exists to answer a question that observation cannot settle: whether a treatment caused an improvement or merely accompanied one. People who receive a treatment differ from those who do not in ways that also affect their outcomes — they may be wealthier, more health-conscious, less severely ill, or simply more likely to seek help — and no amount of statistical adjustment reliably removes differences nobody thought to measure. Allocating treatment by chance does remove them, which is the entire justification for a procedure that otherwise looks perverse.

Blinding addresses a separate problem from randomisation and the two are often conflated. Randomisation makes the groups comparable at the start; blinding keeps them comparable afterwards, by preventing the expectations of patients and assessors from shaping either the experience of treatment or the recording of outcomes. Where blinding is impossible — surgical procedures, physical therapies — the trial can still randomise, and the results carry a known additional uncertainty rather than being worthless.

The comparison group is where most of the difficulty lies. A treatment must be tested against something, and the choice determines what the result means: against nothing, it shows only that something happened; against a dummy treatment, it isolates the specific effect; against the existing best treatment, it answers the question a clinician actually faces. Trials against placebo when an effective treatment exists produce results that are statistically clean and practically uninformative.

What a trial measures determines what can be claimed, and substitution here is the most common way results mislead. A drug shown to improve a laboratory value has not been shown to help anyone feel better or live longer, and the history of medicine includes treatments that reliably improved the measurement while harming the patient. Outcomes that matter to people — survival, function, symptoms — take longer and cost more to measure, which is precisely why they are so often replaced.

Publication introduces a distortion that operates on the whole literature rather than on any single study. Trials with positive results are more likely to be written up, submitted and accepted than those without, so the published record overstates effectiveness even when every individual trial is sound. Registration of trials before they begin was introduced to make the missing ones visible, and it has helped without solving the problem.

None of this means the method should be distrusted, and the fashionable scepticism gets the conclusion wrong. A well-conducted randomised trial remains the most reliable way to establish that a treatment works, and the appropriate response to its limitations is to demand better trials — pre-registered, adequately sized, measuring outcomes that matter, comparing against real alternatives — rather than to fall back on the clinical impression that the method was invented to correct.

passages.title: The Price at the Farm Gate
passages.text:
A smallholder growing coffee, cocoa or tea faces a price determined thousands of kilometres away by forces they cannot observe and would not be able to influence if they could. The crop takes years from planting to first harvest and decades to reach full yield, which means the decision to plant is a bet on a price several years ahead, and the grower has no way of knowing what other growers are planting at the same moment.

That lag produces a cycle that has repeated for as long as records exist. High prices prompt widespread planting; the new trees mature together several years later; supply rises sharply and the price collapses; growers abandon or neglect their trees; supply falls and the price rises again. The cycle is generated by the biology of the plant interacting with the structure of the market, not by anyone's error, and it cannot be removed by better information alone.

Where the money goes along the chain is frequently misdescribed in both directions. The grower receives a small fraction of the retail price, which is true and is usually presented as evidence of exploitation; most of the remainder is genuinely consumed by shipping, roasting or processing, packaging, retail margins and taxes in the consuming country, which is also true. The margin available to redistribute is real but far smaller than the retail-price comparison implies.

The grower's specific vulnerability is not low average prices but variance. A household with no savings, no insurance and no access to credit cannot absorb a bad year, so a price fall forces the sale of assets, the withdrawal of children from school, or the abandonment of the crop — decisions with consequences long outlasting the price movement. Stabilising income matters more to such a household than raising its average, which is the opposite of how support programmes are usually designed.

Certification schemes deliver less than their labels imply and more than their critics allow. Evidence suggests modest price premiums, some improvement in organisation and bargaining position, and requirements that exclude the poorest growers because compliance costs money; the benefits are real, smaller than advertised, and distributed towards growers who were already better placed. Buying certified is a mild good rather than a solution.

What has changed conditions most is unglamorous and rarely campaigned about. Growers who can process their own crop, store it to sell when prices are better, and organise to sell in volume capture a substantially larger share, and the constraints on doing so are storage, working capital and transport rather than goodwill. Investment in those three does more measurable good than any change in what consumers choose at the shelf.
